JEWERS J.

[
1
]

This is an appeal from the master whereby she struck out the
third party claim.  The issue is whether the defendants can have contribution
or indemnity from the third parties with respect to a letter written by the
defendant Asper allegedly defaming the plaintiff.

[
2
]

The third party, Mr. Albert Schultz, wrote an allegedly
defamatory letter to the defendant, Mr. Asper, dated September 12, 1997 and
sent copies to the Jewish Community Campus Board of Directors on September 17,
1997.  In his covering letter to the board, Mr. Schultz made further allegedly
defamatory statements respecting Mr. Asper.

[
3
]

In response to the letters written by Mr. Schultz, Mr. Asper
wrote a letter to Mr. Schultz dated September 15, 1997 in which he allegedly
defamed the plaintiff and sent copies to the same Board of Directors.  He
believed that the earlier letter of Mr. Schultz had already been sent to the
board because that letter indicated on its face that it had been copied to the
board.  (In fact the Schultz letter was not actually sent to the board until
two days later on September 17.)

[
4
]

The plaintiff then brought this action against the defendants for
defamation and the defendants issued a third party claim against the third
parties, claiming special damages by way of contribution and indemnity for any
amount of damages, interest or costs found to be owing by them as a result of
the plaintiff’s allegations in the statement of claim.  They base their claim
on an allegation that the third parties defamed them.  They rely upon Queen’s
Bench Rule 29.01 which is as follows:

Where available

29.01
A defendant may commence a third party
claim against any person who is not a party to the action and who,

(a) is or may be liable to the
defendant for all or part of the plaintiff’s claim;

(b) is or may be liable to the
defendant for an independent claim for damages or other relief arising out of a
transaction or occurrence or series of transactions or occurrences involved in
or related to the main action;  or

(c) should be bound by the
determination of an issue arising between the plaintiff and the defendant.

[
5
]

The master struck out the third party claim on the ground that
the nexus between the plaintiff’s statement of claim and the third party claim
was not sufficient to satisfy the test in Rule 29.01;  that the facts upon
which the plaintiff relies as against the defendants did not issue out of the
relations between the defendants and the third parties because there were none;
and furthermore, the alleged defamation of the defendants did not occur until
after the alleged defamation of the plaintiff and constituted a new transaction
or occurrence.  The master did a thorough review of the facts and the
authorities in her reasons for judgment and I concur with her disposition of
the case.  (The master did not have before her the allegation that Mr. Asper
believed the Schultz letter had been already sent to the board when he wrote
his reply.)

[
6
]

Defence counsel submits that Mr. Asper’s letter was a justifiable
answer to the earlier letter written by Mr. Schultz and was therefore made on
an occasion of qualified privilege which would be a complete defence to the
plaintiff’s claim.  He cites the following articles from
Remedies in Tort

Volume 1, 6-50:

§
126
“A person whose character or conduct has been
attacked is entitled to answer such attack, and any defamatory statements he
may make about the person who attacked him will be privileged, provided they
are published bona fide and are fairly relevant to the accusations made.”

§
127
The test is whether the statement made in response
to the attack upon the defendant’s character was a relevant and reasonable
response and one which the defendant in all the circumstances might honestly
and reasonably have believed to be true and necessary for the purpose of his
vindication, even though it was not so.

§
128
The protection will be lost if in responding to the
attack the defendant goes beyond matters which are reasonably germane to the
accusations which have been brought against him.

[
7
]

Defence counsel also cites the case of
Netupsky et al.
v.
Craig
et al.
, a decision of the Supreme Court of Canada reported in
1972 CanLII 19 (SCC)
, [1972] 28
D.L.R. (3d) 742, in which the above principles were applied.

[
8
]

Mr. Asper was answering an attack by Mr. Schultz – not by the
plaintiff – but there is authority to the effect that some latitude is given in
these cases and if a third party’s character is incidentally besmirched in the
course of answering the plaintiff’s attack, then the privilege will still
apply.  See
Canadian Tort Law, Linden Sixth Edition
, page 705.

[
9
]

The defendants ask for contribution from the third parties.  The
only basis for their doing so would be
s. 2(1)
of
The
Tortfeasors and
Contributory Negligence Act
, R.S.M. 1987, c. T90:

Where damage suffered

2(1)
Where damage is suffered by any person as a
result of a tort, whether a crime or not,

(a) judgment recovered against any
tortfeasor liable in respect of that damage is not a bar to an action against
any other person who would, if sued, have been liable as a joint tortfeasor, in
respect of the same damage;

(b) if more than one action is brought
in respect of that damage by or on behalf of the person by whom it was
suffered, or for the benefit of the estate, or of the wife, husband, parent, or
child, of that person, against tortfeasors liable in respect of the damage
(whether as joint tortfeasors or otherwise), the sums recoverable under the
judgments given in those actions by way of damages shall not in the aggregate
exceed the amount of the damages awarded by the judgment first given; and in
any of those actions, other than that in which judgment is first given, the
plaintiff is not entitled to costs unless the court is of opinion that there
was reasonable ground for bringing the action;

(c) any tortfeasor liable in respect
of that damage may recover contribution from any other tortfeasor who is, or
would if sued have been, liable in respect of the same damage, whether as a
joint tortfeasor or otherwise, so, however, that no person is entitled to
recover contribution from any person entitled to be indemnified by him in
respect of the liability in respect of which the contribution is sought.

[
10
]

Fleming
in
The Law of Torts

Eighth Edition
,
page 262, comments upon the statutory equivalent of
s. 2(1)
(c) as follows:

Contribution may be claimed only from a tortfeasor “who is, or
if sued would have been liable in respect of the same damage.”  Thus he must
either have been sued and held liable or be someone who, though not sued, would
have been liable for it if sued.

[
11
]

In this case, the “damage” is the injury suffered by the
plaintiff by reason of the alleged defamatory statements emanating from Mr.
Asper.  Are the third parties liable – or could they be held liable – for that
same damage?  They have not been held to be liable to the plaintiff;  indeed,
not only has she not sued them but there is no suggestion anywhere in the
pleadings that she would have a cause of action against them for defamation.
The pleadings do not identify any possible cause of action which the plaintiff
would have against the third parties.  The third party claim describes the
alleged defamatory attack by Mr. Schultz on Mr. Asper and then (in
paragraph eleven) goes on to state:

The defendants state that the words alleged by the plaintiff in
the statement of claim to be defamatory were written to defend the defendants’
conduct and character from the unwarranted defamatory attack described in
paragraphs five to ten herein.  It was reasonably foreseeable to the third
parties, or ought to have been, that the defendants would be compelled to
defend their conduct and character in the manner they did.

[
12
]

As noted, that might constitute a defence to the plaintiff’s
action but, apart from that, there is nothing in the third party claim to
suggest how the third parties might also be liable to the plaintiff for the
damage suffered by the plaintiff.  In the absence of any pleading to that
effect, s. 2(1)(c) of
The Tortfeasors and Contributory Negligence Act

can have no application to the third party claim.

[
13
]

The defendants also ask for indemnity from the third parties.  As
to this,
Fleming, supra,
at page 265 states:

The common law’s all-or-nothing ethos ruled out sharing
(contribution) but not a complete shifting (indemnity) of the loss.  An
indemnity was (and is) allowed, generally speaking, whenever anyone, himself
blameless, is held liable for someone else’s tort.  The most obvious
illustration is vicarious liability;  others are where a servant or agent
committed a tort in bona fide execution of orders or where the claimant’s
complicity was procured by the other’s fraud or misrepresentation.  It may also
be based on contract (for example, a specific clause expressly indemnifying a
party against liability for negligence) or on implied warranty.  Thus a retail
seller of defective equipment may have to indemnify his purchaser for the
latter’s liability to his own employee for negligently failing to notice the
defect.

[
14
]

Here again, the defendants have failed to identify any basis upon
which they would be entitled to indemnity from the third parties.  If the
defendants are held liable to the plaintiff, it will be due to their
blameworthy conduct in defaming the plaintiff.  There is no question here of
vicarious liability or strict liability;  nor is there contractual liability.
This is not a case like that of
Allan
v.
Bushnell T.V. Co. Ltd.
,

1968 CanLII 330 (ON CA)
, [1968] 1 O.R. 720 where the defendants alleged defamatory comments were based
on materials and information which the third parties had contracted to supply
to the defendant and where it was alleged that there was an implied obligation
on the part of the third parties to ensure that the information was correct.
There was no relationship of that kind between the defendants and third parties
in this case.  The pleadings simply do not spell out a cause of action as
between the defendants and third parties for indemnity with respect to the
plaintiff’s claim.

[
15
]

In addition to their claim for contribution or indemnity, the
defendants rely upon Rule 29.01(b), enabling them to commence a third party
claim against any person who was not a party to the action and who “is or may be
liable to the defendant for an independent claim for damages or other relief
arising out of a transaction or occurrence or series of transactions or
occurrences involved in or related to the main action;”  … .

[
16
]

They submit that the defendants’ claim against the third parties
could have been brought as “an independent claim for damages” and that it
clearly arose “out of a transaction or occurrence or a series of transactions
or occurrences involved in or related to the main action” in that the third
parties’ defamation of the defendants is already an intrinsic part of the
defence to the main action.

[
17
]

The difficulty with this submission is that the defendants no
longer have an independent claim for damages.  They were certainly entitled to
bring an independent action against the third parties alleging defamation based
on the letter which Mr. Schultz wrote to Mr. Asper;  however, such a claim is
now statute barred except for special damages.  The only special damages which
the defendants could claim against the third parties would be for contribution
or indemnity with respect to the plaintiff’s claim but, as I have held, such a
contribution or indemnity is not available to them.

[
18
]

The defendants also rely upon Rule 29.01(c) which provides for a
third party claim where the third parties “should be bound by the determination
of an issue arising between the plaintiff and the defendant”.  But having
regard to the above conclusions, this subrule can have no possible application
in this case.

[
19
]

The appeal is dismissed with costs.  The defendants’ proposed
amendments to the statement of defence and counterclaim are allowed without
costs.

J.
